You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

The test failure and bug report suggest that curve fitting with a large number of weights (points) causes the creation and copying of a large full matrix, which exhausts memory. This impacts even standard polynomial fitters using multivariate vector optimizers. From the test, we see the PolynomialFitter is used with a large number of observed points (40000). The fit is then computed with an initial guess array. The bug report notes that the problem arises during the passing of a large weight vector to the optimizer, causing large memory overhead.

The test calls PolynomialFitter.fit(double[] guess) at line 241. This method delegates to PolynomialFitter.fit(ParametricUnivariateFunction, double[]) at line 110, which again calls overloads, eventually to a method that performs the fitting. From the snippets retrieved, these calls eventually invoke a method like fit(int maxEval, ParametricUnivariateFunction, double[]) which is one of the key points to investigate. Unfortunately, the fitting method body is not directly retrieved, so the internal behavior of the optimizer call inside PolynomialFitter is unclear.

The root cause, as per the bug report, is that the optimizer receives weight data in a form that forces the N-element vector to be converted into an NxN full matrix, causing excessive memory use for large N (weights). This likely occurs in the optimizer or the wrapper that creates the optimization problem from the observations in PolynomialFitter.

Because the test uses 40000 points and the bug report mentions issues arising with a number of weights around 4120, the problem is consistent with an O(N²) memory issue in the weight or Jacobian matrix creation or copying inside the optimizer call.

Recent bug reports with low similarity do not provide additional clues.

Diagnosis:

- The failing test uses a large sample size (40000 points) to do polynomial fitting.
- PolynomialFitter.fit calls a multivariate vector optimizer internally.
- The optimizer is given weights or data in such a way that creates NxN full matrices even when only N weights are passed.
- This behavior causes excessive memory usage and failure for large N.
- This bug is inherent in how weights are handled or converted inside the optimizer or in PolynomialFitter.
- The current code copies/converts weight vectors into full matrices in a way that scales poorly.

This indicates a design flaw in optimizer weight handling, requiring changes either in PolynomialFitter or the optimizer wrappers to avoid creating large NxN matrices for vector weights, especially when they are diagonal (independent weights for each point).

Hence, the cause of the bug is that PolynomialFitter uses an optimizer that is not efficient with large weight vectors, transforming them into large dense matrices, exhausting memory.

This matches the test fail and current bug report description exactly.

The fix should target weight handling in either PolynomialFitter or the multivariate vector optimizer to avoid unnecessary NxN matrix creation.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
